summary: Defines what XMPP addresses look like, including names that use characters beyond plain ASCII, such as letters from other writing systems. It relies on the PRECIS approach to internationalized strings. It replaces RFC 6122.

eli5.summary: An XMPP address is like a home address for chat. This says how to write one correctly, even when the name uses letters from many languages.

subtitle: What an XMPP address (a JID) looks like, and how names in any script are prepared and compared safely.

tldr.problem: XMPP addresses had relied on the stringprep technology for non-ASCII characters, which the IETF was moving away from for internationalized domain names.
tldr.mechanism: A JID is split into an optional localpart, a required domainpart and an optional resourcepart. The domainpart follows IDNA2008, the localpart uses the PRECIS UsernameCaseMapped profile, and the resourcepart uses the PRECIS OpaqueString profile.
tldr.outcome: This document obsoletes RFC 6122 and has been updated by RFC 9844. Previously valid JIDs might no longer be valid, so operators are told to test before migrating.

today: RFC 7622 is a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 6122, and it has been updated by RFC 9844. Read the two together for the current rules.

sections.title: Why the Address Format Changed
sections.content:
The Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP, RFC 6120) streams XML data in close to real time between network-aware entities. Its address format came from the Jabber community in 1999, was described in XEP-0029 in 2002, and was defined by RFC 3920 in 2004 and RFC 6122 in 2011.

Those RFCs used stringprep to prepare and compare non-ASCII characters. Following the movement of internationalized domain names away from stringprep, this document drops that dependency and builds on the PRECIS framework of RFC 7564.

Every attempt was made to keep the characters allowed under stringprep allowed under PRECIS, but there is no guarantee of strict backward compatibility. Previously valid JIDs might become invalid, or the reverse, so operators are advised to test carefully before migrating accounts and other data.
sections.eli5: The old way of checking letters in names was being retired. This is the new rulebook, and it is a little different, so chat providers should test before switching.

sections.title: The Shape of a JID
sections.content:
An XMPP entity is anything that can communicate using XMPP. For historical reasons its network address is called a JID. A valid JID is a string of Unicode code points, encoded as UTF-8, made of a localpart, a domainpart and a resourcepart. The first two are separated by @ and the last two by /, as in juliet@example.com/balcony.

The ABNF is jid = [ localpart "@" ] domainpart [ "/" resourcepart ]. Each part is 1 to 1023 octets long, which gives a maximum total of 3071 octets including the separators. The limits count bytes, not characters, because UTF-8 can use more than one octet per character.

When splitting a JID, an implementation needs to find the @ and / separators before applying any transformation that might decompose some code points into those characters. The domainpart is what is left after removing everything from the first / to the end, then everything up to the first @. This order matters: in a.example.com/b@example.net the @ belongs to the resourcepart.
sections.eli5: A chat address has up to three parts: a person's name, the building they live in, and which door of the house you are using. The building is the only part you cannot leave out.

sections.title: The Three Parts and Their Rules
sections.content:
Domainpart. The only required part. It usually names the home server, but may name another service such as a multi-user chat service. It MUST be a fully qualified domain name, an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address (in square brackets), or an unqualified hostname. A final dot is stripped before routing or comparing. In general it is an Internationalized Domain Name under IDNA2008, and must consist of NR-LDH labels or U-labels, so A-labels are converted to U-labels. Enforcement also applies normalization, case-mapping and width-mapping rules, and two domainparts are equal if they match octet for octet after that.

Localpart. Typically an account or a chatroom. It is an instance of the UsernameCaseMapped profile of the PRECIS IdentifierClass from RFC 7613. XMPP further forbids eight characters in a localpart: ", &, ', /, :, <, > and @.

Resourcepart. Typically a specific connection (a device or location) or an occupant of a chatroom. It is an instance of the OpaqueString profile of the PRECIS FreeformClass. Entities SHOULD treat it as an opaque string and not read meaning into it. The / does not make addresses hierarchical, and @ is allowed inside a resourcepart.
sections.eli5: Each part has its own spelling rules. The name is strict, the building follows domain-name rules, and the door label is the most relaxed, so even a chess piece symbol is allowed there.

sections.title: Legal and Illegal Examples
sections.content:
Section 3.5 lists valid and invalid JIDs. Valid ones include a bare JID juliet@example.com, a full JID juliet@example.com/foo, a resourcepart with a space, and a resourcepart containing @.

The examples make several points. A localpart with the German character esszett differs from one with ss, so a server needs its own policy if it wants to block one when the other is registered. Greek capital sigma and small sigma match after case-mapping, but small final sigma does not match either. A chess king symbol is allowed in a resourcepart but not in a localpart. Roman numeral four is not allowed in a localpart because it has a compatibility equivalent.

Invalid strings include quoted localparts, a space in a localpart (which can be written \20 using the JID Escaping extension), a leading space in a resourcepart, an empty localpart, and addresses with no domainpart.
sections.eli5: Some names that look odd are fine, and some that look fine are not. Two words that sound alike, like the German double-s letter and plain ss, still count as different names.

sections.title: Who Enforces the Rules
sections.content:
Enforcement means applying all the rules in this document. It is the responsibility of XMPP servers. Clients SHOULD prepare JIDs before putting them into XML streams, but servers MUST enforce the rules wherever possible and reject violating stanzas, returning a <jid-malformed/> error to the sender.

Servers are encouraged to be liberal: first map characters where possible (width mapping, case mapping, normalization and so on) and accept the mapped string; if mapping is not possible, reject it.

The document defines JID slots, localpart slots and resourcepart slots: XML elements or attributes designated for carrying a complete JID, a localpart or a resourcepart. A server enforces the rules on slots it handles itself or uses for routing, such as the to attribute of a stanza or the <resource/> child of <bind/>. For slots meant for communication between other entities, such as the Jingle initiator attribute, those entities SHOULD enforce the rules themselves.
sections.eli5: The post office (the server) checks every address on letters it handles. For notes passed between friends inside the envelope, the friends should check each other's spelling.

sections.title: Security: Forging and Mimicking
sections.content:
The security considerations of PRECIS (RFC 7564), IDNA (RFC 5890) and Unicode (UTS 39) apply. The document then separates two kinds of address spoofing.

Forging is sending a stanza whose from address does not match the sender's authenticated account. It is difficult in XMPP because sending servers stamp from addresses and receiving servers verify sending domains. It remains possible with a poorly implemented or malicious server, so an outside entity can authenticate only the domainpart of a JID with any level of assurance. End-to-end signing or encryption could help.

Mimicking is using a legitimate account whose JID looks the same to a human as another JID. For example, ju1iet with the digit one can look like juliet. IDNA and PRECIS do not solve visually similar characters, so domainparts, localparts and resourceparts can all be mimicked, with effects such as users joining a fake chat service or sending a private message to the wrong person in a chatroom. Services and clients are strongly encouraged to adopt consistent policies on registering, storing and showing look-alike characters, following RFC 7564.
sections.eli5: A trickster might sign up as ju1iet to pass as juliet. The computer sees different names, but your eyes may not, so providers need rules to spot look-alikes.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 6122
sections.content:
Appendix A lists the substantive changes:

  • Domainparts now use IDNA2008 instead of IDNA2003, and internationalized labels must be U-labels instead of "should be" U-labels.
  • Localparts use the PRECIS UsernameCaseMapped profile instead of the stringprep Nodeprep profile.
  • Resourceparts use the PRECIS OpaqueString profile instead of the stringprep Resourceprep profile.
  • Fullwidth and halfwidth characters must be mapped to their decomposition mappings, and Unicode Normalization Form C replaces Form KC.
  • Servers must enforce the address-formatting rules.

For compatibility, many existing deployments still support IDNA2003, Nodeprep and Resourceprep. IANA marked the Nodeprep and Resourceprep stringprep profiles as Not Current.
sections.eli5: The spelling checker for names was swapped for a newer one, and the servers now have to use it on every address they see.

data.title: JID grammar
data.code:
jid          = [ localpart "@" ] domainpart [ "/" resourcepart ]
localpart    = 1*1023(userbyte)
domainpart   = IP-literal / IPv4address / ifqdn
resourcepart = 1*1023(opaquebyte)

cells: IDNA2008 (or an IP address or unqualified hostname)
